en: The Scripture on the Staff as a Ladder for Attaining the Path;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “You all should receive and uphold the *khakkhara* staff.”
Why is this? The Buddhas of the past held the mendicant’s staff; the Buddhas of the future will hold the mendicant’s staff; and the Buddhas of the present also hold this staff.
Just as I, having now attained Buddhahood as a World-Honored One, also hold this staff which should be maintained,
so too have the Buddhas of the past, future, and present taught their disciples to hold the khakkhara staff.
Therefore, I have now attained Buddhahood as a World-Honored One and, in accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, instruct you thus:
You all should now receive and uphold the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*). Why is this?
This alms-staff is called the Staff of Wisdom and is also called the Staff of Virtue.
It is named the Staff of Wisdom because it manifests holy insight;
it is called the Staff of Virtue because it practices the root of merit.

Such a staff is the outward manifestation of the sages, the clear record of the worthy ones, the upright banner of the Dharma for entering the Way, and the pillar that establishes the resolve for the meaning of mindfulness; therefore, all of you should hold it in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Kāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes so as to bare his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt on his right knee, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is called a *khakkhara* staff?
How should it be received and maintained?
Thus we ask, World-Honored One!
"We pray that you will expound it in detail, so that we may practice it accordingly.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively and reflect well!"
I shall explain it for you.
As for what is called the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), "khak" means light.
By relying on this staff, one is able to eliminate afflictions (*kleśa*) and emerge from the triple world; therefore, it is called "light."
The *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) signifies clarity.
One who holds the staff attains the clarity of wisdom; therefore, it is called "clarity.
*Khakkhara* also means "not turning back."
One who holds this staff is able to transcend the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and is no longer defiled by attachment; therefore, it is called "non-retrogression" (*avivarta*).
"Chestu" (the staff) signifies "awakening" (*xing*).

One who holds this staff awakens to suffering, emptiness, and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the triple world, clearly understanding the Four Noble Truths and the twelvefold chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); therefore, it is called "awakening."
The term *khakkhara* signifies "not arrogant.
One who holds this staff eliminates and severs the karma of arrogance; therefore, it is called "not arrogant.
*Khakkhara* also signifies "sparse" or "distant."

One who holds this staff is distant from the five desires, severs the fetters of craving and attachment, disperses and destroys the aggregates (*skandhas*), remains far removed from the five hindrances (*nīvaranas*), and directs their aspiration toward *nirvāṇa*. Because they distance themselves from conditioned karma (*saṃskṛta-karman*), it is called "distancing" (*sū*).
"Taking up" means to gather; one who holds this staff gathers the jewels of the Buddhas' precepts, concentration, and wisdom, thereby attaining liberation; hence it is called "taking up."
"Xi" (錫) means "accomplishment.

One who holds this staff accomplishes the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas; by practicing according to the teachings, they ensure nothing is deficient or diminished, fully achieving everything. Therefore, it is called "accomplishment."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"In this way, the meaning of the word 'khakkhara' is vast and manifold; it cannot be fully set forth. For now, you should simply uphold it in this manner."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Such is the meaning of this mendicant’s staff; what is the meaning of the 'staff of wisdom,' and so forth, up to the resolve for the meaning of establishing mindfulness?"
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound upon this for us.
The Buddha said:

"As for this khakkhara: it is for the practitioner who cultivates wisdom, who extensively cultivates great learning, who understands the mundane and the supramundane, who discriminates between the wholesome and the unwholesome, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing; because their clear knowledge is unimpeded and their wisdom is perfected, it is called the 'Wisdom Staff'."

"Because one upholds the prohibitive precepts, practices patience and meditative concentration, maintains a single-minded focus without distraction, constantly cultivates meritorious deeds, and never slackens—acting as if putting out a fire on one's own head—it is therefore called the 'Staff of Virtue'."
“Holding this staff, such a person is internally endowed with sixteen practices (namely, the Four Truths:
suffering, origin, cessation, and the path;
and the four [immeasurables]:”
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The four dhyānas:
the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
The four formless absorptions (namely:

the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), as well as the full possession of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (that is,
the thirty-seven aids to the path).
Within this Dharma, one discerns with perfect clarity, realizing it through personal testimony and not following mere sounds;

within this Dharma, one sports freely, entering the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—with sovereign ease and without hindrance; such a person is called a noble one (ārya).
Internally possessing such virtues and externally holding the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), this person is marked as one who must surely possess sagely merit.

Endowed with the precepts, concentration, patience, and wisdom, as well as the three insights (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), these qualities are all fully present. By using the staff to record and signify this person, others are led to conceive reverence; therefore, it is called "the outward sign of the sage."
"Regarding 'the wise person’s clear recollection':
because he possesses the nature of wisdom within, he is called a wise person.

To clearly recollect that this person possesses the nature of wisdom within, has cultivated the roots of merit, progresses in the Dharma, and has perfected a virtuous mind—therefore, it is called 'the wise person’s clear recollection.'"

"Before long, this person will achieve wisdom, enter the realm of the unconditioned, and abide in profound stillness and tranquility—the blissful nirvana and the path of the ultimate truth; therefore, they are called 'one who proceeds toward the Dharma-banner of the Path.'"
"One who establishes the resolve for the meaning of mindfulness possesses a staff with three rings.
Seeing the weight of these three rings, one contemplates the suffering and affliction of the three miserable realms (trāya), thereby cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom;
contemplating the three calamities of old age, sickness, and death, one eliminates the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion."

Reflecting upon the impermanence of the three realms, one places deep faith in the Triple Gem, eliminates the three evil destinies, severs the three outflows, and purifies the three karmas. Desiring to possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), enter the three gates of liberation, attain the three foundations of mindfulness, and master the threefold penetrating wisdom, one establishes the three partitions to signify this progressive layering.

"Furthermore, as for the four prongs: they are established to sever the four modes of birth, to contemplate the Four Noble Truths, to cultivate the Four Immeasurables, to enter the Four Dhyānas, to purify the Four Formless Attainments, to clarify the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, to strengthen the Four Right Efforts, and to attain the Four Bases of Psychic Power; hence there are four edges."

"Passing through the five internal partitions is used to sever the suffering and cyclic rebirth of the five paths; by cultivating the five faculties, possessing the five powers, removing the five hindrances, dispersing the five aggregates, and attaining the fivefold Dharma-body, the number five is established."

"The twelve rings signify using mindfulness of the twelve links of dependent origination to achieve unimpeded penetration; by practicing the twelve gates of dhyāna, one causes the mind to be free from affliction."
"The three layers and four sides combined total seven; by recollecting the Tathāgata’s seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), one accomplishes the seven noble riches (*saptadhanas*).

The perforated partitions number eight, used for recollecting the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); one thereby attains the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and eliminates the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), which is why there are eight."
"In brief, such is the meaning of the khakkhara staff!
You should uphold it well.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
It shall be according to the holy Dharma and its teachings.
At that time, Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time all the same?
The Buddha said:
"The staffs are identical in this regard; however, as for their usage, they differ.
Some have four prongs, while others have two; the number of rings is no different.
Yet today, I employ the teaching of the four-pronged staff with twelve rings."

As for the two-pronged [vajra], it was established by Tathāgata Kāśyapa to cause all sentient beings to keep the two truths (the conventional truth and the ultimate truth) in mind, thereby establishing their meaning.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the Venerable Kāśyapa, the assembly of twelve hundred,
and the entire great congregation were all filled with joy; they received it upon their heads and respectfully put it into practice.
In the general structure of this dharma, the upper platform corresponds to heaven, the lower platform corresponds to earth, and the four legs correspond to the Four Heavenly Kings;
the twelve rings correspond to the twelve links of dependent origination. Encompassing heaven, earth, humans, and the heavens above and below, there is nothing that is not fully contained within it.
Whenever one gives rise to compassion, it broadly generates the myriad practices; since all things do not conform to this [without it], it serves as the foundation for initiating goodness.
When holding this staff according to the Dharma, carry it across heaven and support it against the earth, placing it beneath the left side of the ribs and securing it with the little finger;
ensure that both ends are level and upright, without allowing them to be uneven.
If it sounds, it sounds constantly, not allowing the sound to cease;
its tone is even, subtle, and harmonious, always remaining as it was at the beginning.
If there is no sound at the beginning, it ensures that no sound occurs throughout the entire course of the practice.
If there is sound at the beginning, ensure that sound continues throughout the entire course of the recitation;
furthermore, the volume must remain uniform, neither too loud nor too soft.
The monks shall place their left foot forward, and the nuns shall place their right foot forward.
One must not let it touch the ground;

if the donor does not provide it, one may go as near as three houses or as far as seven houses. If it cannot be obtained there, one must not go further; to exceed that limit is contrary to the Dharma of the practitioner.
If one obtains food within the prescribed time limit, one should carry it on a staff and suspend it from a tree so that it does not touch the ground;
if there is no tree and it must be placed on the ground, one should set it on a level spot so that it does not lean or tip over.
When sleeping, place the staff so that it is aligned with the body; set it behind the bed, level with the body, ensuring it does not lean forward or backward.
When carrying it while walking or resting, the head of the staff should always face the sun; do not allow it to be inverted or turned away.
To hold this staff is to hold the body of the Buddha; all ten thousand practices are contained within it, which is to say, holding heaven and supporting earth.
Furthermore, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as a means of protecting the entire person.
Just as it tilts, all myriad things likewise tilt;
just as it is level and upright, it causes all sentient beings to dwell in peace and non-action.
If the platform were to touch the ground when lowered, it would cause the suffering of sentient beings in the three miserable realms to increase even more intensely;
if it did not touch the ground, it would enable those beings in the three miserable realms to be delivered from them because of this.
If one holds [the teachings] erroneously, it will run counter to the world and cause the practitioner’s mind to become confused;
if one can maintain them correctly, both self and others will benefit.
By maintaining them in this way, one will fully manifest the support of dignified conduct in all comings and goings, and subsequently attain the fruit, swiftly achieving perfect enlightenment.
Regarding the rules for the majestic deportment of carrying the *khakkhara* (monk’s staff), there are twenty-five matters.
There are ten matters concerning the method of carrying the *khakkhara*:
first, because there may be insects in the ground.
Second, because of being aged and infirm;
third, because of having crossed over [a boundary];
fourth, because one may not hold [the bowl] in hand while moving forward or backward.
Fifth, one must not carry a staff upon the shoulder.
Sixth, one must not carry it across the shoulder with both hands hanging down at the ends.
Seventh, when entering or exiting and seeing a Buddha image, one must not allow any sound to be made.
Eighth, the staff must not enter the assembly.
Ninth, one must not carry it about recklessly behind the dwelling.
Tenth, the staff must not be carried beyond midday.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when invited to a distant place, one may leave after midday if one has stayed overnight;
second, when visiting the home of someone who is ill or emaciated, one may leave after midday.
Third, one may go out after midday to escort those who have passed away.
Fourth, one may go out after midday at the invitation of non-Buddhists.
Fifth, one must not point with a staff at people or draw figures or characters on the ground.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, when the three masters go out together, one must not carry a staff along with them.
Second, when four persons travel together, except for the *upādhyāya*, no one may carry [a staff] universally.
Third, upon arriving at the gate of a donor, one should properly rectify one’s deportment.
Fourth, having entered the gate of a donor, one should shake oneself three times; if no [alms] are given, one should proceed from there to another house.
Fifth, when the donor comes out, one should hold the staff and place it against the center of the left elbow.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, the staff must always remain within one's own room and may not be separated from one's person.
Second, one must not allow the lower end to touch the ground.
Third, one must not allow the staff to be wrapped in raw cloth.
Fourth, it must be polished and wiped clean every day.
Fifth, when one wishes to take up the staff, it should be received from the side of a *śrāmaṇera*; if there is no *śrāmaṇera*, it may also be received from a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
The four-pronged head of the *khakkhara* corresponds to the Four Noble Truths; the rings correspond to the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
and the central ring signifies the meaning of the Middle Way.
The second should be Mount Sumeru; the central tree should be in the void, with its lower roots extending down to Mount Sumeru.
This is the Dharma of the śramaṇa: by understanding emptiness one attains the Way, and by maintaining this clarity, one awakens all sentient beings in the world.
O Bhikṣus! Practice this with a sincere heart.

This *Jītu-dao-ticheng-xizhang-jing* (Sūtra on the Staff as a Ladder to the Path), also known as the *Chizhizhang-fa* (Method of Carrying the Staff), has been re-translated based on the Indian Tripiṭaka so that future generations may read and examine it to understand its origins and lineage. There are twenty-five matters of dignified conduct (*vinaya*) regarding the staff.
There are twenty-five reasons for carrying a *khakkhara* (monastic staff):
first, for the sake of [warning] snakes and insects;
second, for the sake of old age.
Third, for the sake of begging for alms.
Fourth, when entering or exiting to see a Buddha image, one must not allow the head to make a sound.
Fifth, one must not carry a staff when entering the assembly.
Sixth, one must not go out with the staff again after midday.
Seventh, one must not carry it on the shoulder with the hands hanging from both ends.
Eighth, one must not place it across the knees with the hands hanging from both ends.
Ninth, one must not swing the staff back and forth with the hands.
Tenth, one must not carry it behind the dwelling.
Eleventh, one must not carry it in front of or behind the three teachers; once the staff has been set aside, one must not follow after them carrying it again.
Twelfth, if four people are traveling together and one person is already carrying [the staff], another shall not carry it as well.
Thirteenth, if they arrive at the house of a donor, they must not leave the staff out of their possession.
Fourteenth, when arriving at the gate of a person's residence, one should shake [the bowl] three times; if they do not come out, one should proceed to another house.
Fifteenth, when the host comes out, one should hold the staff against the left elbow and carry it tucked under the arm.
Sixteenth, if one enters a room, one must not allow it to touch the ground.
Seventeenth, one should keep it close to one's own bed.
Eighteenth, one should frequently take it up and wipe it clean.
Nineteenth, one must not allow hair to grow on the head.
Twentieth, when intending to travel, one should receive [permission] from a śrāmaṇera or a layperson.
Twenty-first, when staying overnight at the house of a sick person, one should obtain a staff for evening.
Twenty-second: One who wishes to escort someone far away should possess an evening staff.
Twenty-third: One who travels to a distant place for an invitation and stays overnight should possess an evening staff.
Twenty-fourth: When going out to meet those who come from afar, one should carry a staff in the evening.
Twenty-fifth: One should always remain close [to others] oneself; one must not point at people or draw figures or write characters on the ground.
The Method for Carrying the Śikya Staff (Khaṭvāṅga)
